message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and other compute‑heavy tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core is lightweight and optimized for throughput rather than latency. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple instruction set focused on arithmetic and data movement; often uses vector instructions. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, strong support for random access patterns. | Smaller per‑core caches, relies heavily on massive shared memory and fast on‑chip SRAM; best suited for regular, predictable memory access patterns. |
| **Parallelism** | Parallelism is limited by the number of cores and hyper‑threading; each core can execute one thread at a time. | Massive data‑parallelism: thousands of threads run simultaneously, all executing the same instruction stream on different data. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services, database queries, web servers. | Highly parallel tasks: image/video processing, physics simulations, deep‑learning inference/training, scientific calculations. |
| **Power & cost** | More power‑hungry per core, higher cost per core due to complexity. | Lower power per core, cheaper to produce en masse; overall cost depends on performance needs. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, irregular tasks quickly, while a GPU shines when you have a huge amount of similar operations that can be performed in parallel. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU manages the system and orchestrates tasks, and the GPU accelerates the heavy lifting for specific workloads.
